title: Limiting negative gearing to new builds would make housing materially more affordable
oneLiner: Removing the tax advantage for investors in existing homes would take heat out of the market first-home buyers compete in.
body: Investors and first-home buyers bid for the same established dwellings. Removing a concession available only to one side would, proponents argue, shift enough demand to make a visible difference to prices and to who wins at auction.
contextBackground: This is the claim most proponents actually care about. It is separated here from the proposal itself because one can support the proposal on fairness grounds while accepting the price effect would be small.
contextDisagreement: The best available modelling finds a price effect of a few per cent. Whether that is 'material' is partly a judgement, and partly depends on whether one counts the effect on who buys rather than just on price.

evidenceItems.citation: Grattan Institute, Hot property: negative gearing and capital gains tax reform (2016) — modelled price effects

otherClaim.title: Parliament should pass the 2026 budget's restriction of negative gearing to newly built homes

claimItself.title: Parliament should pass the 2026 budget's restriction of negative gearing to newly built homes
claimItself.oneLiner: The policy is now a bill before the Senate: negative gearing for new builds only from July 2027, existing investors grandfathered, and a reworked capital gains discount alongside it.
claimItself.body: The 12 May 2026 budget restricted negative gearing to newly built residential property for investments made after budget night, with effect from 1 July 2027, and replaced the 50 per cent capital gains discount with an inflation-based discount and a 30 per cent floor. Anyone using the concessions before budget night keeps them. A Senate inquiry took evidence in June 2026.

ownArguments.text: The large majority of investor housing loans finance established dwellings rather than new construction

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
ownArguments.text: Winding back negative gearing would push rents up as investors leave the market

otherClaim.title: Treasury estimates the 2026 changes would raise rents by less than $2 a week for a household on the median rent

claimItself.title: Treasury estimates the 2026 changes would raise rents by less than $2 a week for a household on the median rent
claimItself.oneLiner: The official estimate of the rent effect is small.
claimItself.body: Treasury's budget modelling puts the rent effect of restricting negative gearing and reworking the capital gains discount at under $2 a week at the median, and estimates about 35,000 fewer homes over a decade, more than offset in its view by the budget's supply measures. Its secretary told the Senate the measures mainly shift ownership from investors to owner-occupiers.

otherClaim.title: Grattan Institute modelling found that limiting negative gearing and halving the capital gains discount would lower house prices by about 2 per cent

claimItself.title: Grattan Institute modelling found that limiting negative gearing and halving the capital gains discount would lower house prices by about 2 per cent
claimItself.oneLiner: The most-cited independent estimate puts the price effect in the low single digits.
claimItself.body: Grattan's 2016 analysis estimated that both reforms together would reduce prices by roughly 2 per cent and reduce the share of homes bought by investors, with little effect on rents. It is the figure most often quoted on both sides.
